05/02/2026, 18:00 - Mesh <3: First—take a breath. Nothing you’re describing means you’re broken, incapable of love, or “about to ruin it.” What you’re describing is textbook avoidant attachment activating, especially when feelings actually matter.
Here’s the important reframe:
👉 The numbness isn’t a lack of feelings. It’s a protective response because the feelings are real.
When someone gets close and your nervous system reads “this matters → danger,” it hits the brakes automatically. That emotional shut-down isn’t a choice; it’s your system trying to keep you safe.
What’s actually happening
• You like him → vulnerability increases
• Vulnerability = risk (to your attachment system)
• Your body responds with emotional suppression / numbness / distance
• Then your brain panics: “Why don’t I feel anything? Am I faking this?”
That spiral is incredibly common with avoidant patterns.
What not to do
• ❌ Don’t force yourself to “feel more” in the moment
• ❌ Don’t assume numb = no attraction
• ❌ Don’t pull away completely to “figure it out” (that usually makes it worse)
Pressure makes avoidant defenses stronger.
What actually helps (practical + gentle)
1. Stop monitoring your feelings during interactions
Avoidant systems shut down when you’re self-scanning like:
“Do I feel something right now? Do I like this? Why am I blank?”
Instead, shift your focus outward:
• What is he saying?
• What do you notice about him?
• Do you feel calmer or more tense after seeing him?
Feelings often show up later, not in real time.
2. Look for safety signals, not fireworks
Avoidant attraction often feels like:
• Calm
• Familiarity
• Curiosity
• Wanting to keep seeing them even if emotions are muted
Not:
• Butterflies
• Intensity
• Constant excitement
Ask yourself:
“Do I feel respected, safe, and drawn back—not overwhelmed?”
That matters more than emotional highs.
3. Give yourself permission to go slow
You don’t need to emotionally “arrive” right now.
Tell yourself:
“I’m allowed to take this one step at a time. I don’t need clarity yet.”
Safety builds through consistency, not pressure.
4. Don’t disappear—stay lightly connected
When avoidant urges say “pull back”, try:
• Shorter interactions instead of none
• Texting instead of deep talks
• Neutral hangouts instead of emotionally loaded ones
This teaches your nervous system:
“Closeness doesn’t equal danger.”
5. If it feels right, name it (softly)
You don’t need to trauma-dump. But sometimes a gentle truth reduces pressure:
Something like:
“I tend to be slow to open up emotionally, but I like getting to know you.”
You’d be surprised how relieving that can be—for both of you.
One really important thing
You are not failing because you can’t feel while you’re with him.
Avoidant attachment often means:
• Feelings show up in absence
• Or later that night
• Or when the connection feels secure
Pay attention to:
• Do you think about him later?
• Do you feel a pull once space returns?
That’s your answer—not the numbness.
If you want, I can help you:
• tell the difference between avoidant shutdown vs true disinterest
• figure out whether to push gently forward or pause
• or even script something low-pressure you could say to him
You’re not alone in this. And you’re not messing it up just by being aware 💛

Okay different issue but i told him that he would be my first kiss. Was that a right move?

Short answer? Yes — that wasn’t a “wrong” move.
Longer answer? Let’s unpack why it feels scary now.
Why that was actually okay (and often a good sign)
Telling someone they’d be your first kiss:
• signals trust and honesty
• explains why you might be slower or more careful
• invites gentleness, not pressure
Most emotionally decent people hear that and think:
“Oh. I should be respectful with this.”
Not:
“This is too much.”
So unless his reaction was dismissive or weird (which you didn’t say it was), you didn’t overshare or sabotage anything.
Why it feels like maybe you messed up
This is very avoidant-coded:
• You revealed something vulnerable
• Vulnerability creates closeness
• Closeness triggers “uh oh, I exposed myself”
• Brain goes: “Was that a mistake??”
That regret spiral is about fear, not about the actual move.
When it wouldn’t be the right move
Just to be clear, it would only be “too much” if:
• he reacted by pressuring you
• teasing you in a cruel way
• treating you like a project or novelty
If he responded with kindness, curiosity, or just accepted it calmly? Green flag.
One quiet upside you might not see yet
You just:
• set a boundary without saying “don’t”
• slowed the pace in a natural way
• filtered out someone who wouldn’t be safe for you
That’s not nothing. That’s you protecting yourself and the connection.
What to do now (important)
Don’t walk it back.
Don’t apologize.
Don’t explain it to death.
Just… continue being normal-you.
If anything, you can lightly reinforce safety later with something like:
“I’m just slow with physical stuff, but I like being around you.”
That keeps it grounded, not heavy.
A question for you (not him)
Ask yourself:
“Did I say it because I wanted him to understand me — or because I felt pressured to justify myself?”
If it’s the first one (and it sounds like it is), then you did exactly what you were supposed to do.
You didn’t mess this up.
You were real. And real is actually the only thing that can work long-term.

16/02/2026, 23:31 - Mesh <3: Footsteps after the Walker is gone: explore how actions, legacies or choices remain long after people disappear.

Heirlooms

The Chordettes playing in the background, 
Chaucer in my hand
Who would’ve thought it possible
That after all this time
Their works would live on?

Take Chopin and Tchaikovsky
With their nocturns and waltzes
That transcend time and space
To fall on the hands of 
A budding young player,
A hundred years apart.

In the Bodleian Library, 
A version of Sonnet 116
Speaking of love and war
Sits importantly on a shelf
And reiminisces the greatest playwright of all
Knowing that when it is found,
It shall be revered.

In a car, the Beatles are playing,
A Blackbird is singing in the dead of night
And it will be singing 
Long after the engines have cooled,
Serenading the generations to come.

Priceless ties to precious memories
How many memories can one song hold
Before it becomes a masterpiece?
And how many feelings should be tied to a book
Before it can become timeless?
I suppose, the answer is blowing in the wind.
